title: Code Detectors Have a Half-Life: Obsolescence and Metric Illusions in LLM-Generated Code Detection

paper.title: Code Detectors Have a Half-Life: Obsolescence and Metric Illusions in LLM-Generated Code Detection
paper.abstract:
Abstract. Code detectors can become obsolete as code-generating models
evolve: a detector validated on one generation of models may not
transfer to the next. We call this limited useful life a detector half-
life. We evaluate eight general-purpose LLM judges and three dedicated detectors on human-written code and code produced by seven generators across C++, Java, and Python. Our results reveal two problems. First, performance varies considerably across generators and prompting strategies, suggesting that some detectors rely on generator-specific patterns rather than general evidence of code provenance. Second, accuracy can conceal severe prediction bias. DetectCodeGPT and GPT-Sniffer achieved an accuracy of 0.50 but an F 1 F_{1} score of 0.00 across all generators because they classified almost every sample as AI-generated. However, general-purpose LLM judges achieved stronger accuracy and F 1 F_{1} scores. Our results show that general-purpose LLMs are promising training-free judges of code provenance and can outperform dedicated detectors. However, their reliability depends on the judge model, the code generator, and the prompting strategy. We therefore recommend evaluating LLM judges across multiple generators and reporting macro- F 1 F_{1} alongside class-specific precision and recall.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: LLMs now generate, complete, and refactor source code ( Zan et al., 2023 ; Hou et al., 2024 ) . Undisclosed use can undermine educational assessment, complicate license and intellectual-property review, and make security-sensitive code harder to vet, as LLMs can reproduce insecure patterns from their training data. Reliable code-provenance detection is therefore increasingly important. However, code is harder to classify than natural language because syntactic constraints compress the token-distribution differences used by text detectors ( Shi et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2024 ) . Existing detectors commonly require white-box access, labeled data, or dedicated infrastructure ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Nguyen et al., 2024 ; JianWang et al., 2024 ) . More fundamentally, they are validated against a bounded set of generators. As generator families and output styles evolve, reported performance may expire a limitation we call detector half-life . Furthermore, the common reliance of detectors on accuracy creates a second risk: on a balanced dataset, a detector that predicts only one class still scores 0.50. General-purpose LLMs offer a simple alternative. Instead of training a separate classifier, an LLM can be asked whether a program was written by a human or generated by another model. This makes LLM judges attractive as training-free detectors. However, LLM judgments can be affected by model preferences, prompting choices, and superficial code features ( Pan et al., 2024 ; Moon et al., 2026 ) . This paper studies both the promise and the limits of LLM judges. We compare eight general-purpose LLMs with three dedicated detectors across seven code generators and three programming languages. Specifically, we ask how accurately general-purpose LLMs distinguish AI-generated from human-written code without task-specific training ( RQ1 ), and how lexical, structural, and lexico-semantic guidance affect their accuracy and decision biases ( RQ2 ). We make the following contribution. ❶ evidence that current code detectors have a half-life; ❷ an empirical demonstration that accuracy can mask detector collapse; and ❸ a cross-generator evaluation of LLM judges as a more adaptable, though still imperfect, alternative.

sections.heading: 2. Related Works
sections.text: LLM-output detection uses trained classifiers, zero-shot statistics, or watermarking ( Nguyen et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Mitchell et al., 2023 ) . Code-specific variants add stylistic, task-conditioned, finetuned, or signal-based features ( Shi et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2024 ; Skurla et al., 2026 ; Yao et al., 2026 ) . These methods are typically tested on a fixed set of existing generators and reported mainly using accuracy, leaving their robustness to newer generators and susceptibility to class collapse unclear. General-purpose LLM evaluators avoid detector training ( Pan et al., 2024 ) and may adapt as foundation models improve, though prompt and judge biases remain ( Moon et al., 2026 ) . Unlike Pan et al. (2024) , who evaluate a single prompting strategy, we systematically compare direct and feature-guided prompting across eight judges, seven generators, and three languages, revealing that prompting strategy interacts with judge identity in ways a single-condition evaluation cannot expose.

sections.heading: 3. Methodology
sections.text: We use the AI-Human-Generated-Program-Code Dataset ( Idrisov and Schlippe, 2024 ) : 18 programming problems (C++, Python, Java), each paired with one human-written solution and one AI-generated solution per generator (StarCoder, ChatGPT, Bing AI Chat, Code Llama, CodeWhisperer, GitHub Copilot, InstructCodeT5+), yielding 18 human and 18 × 7 = 126 18{\times}7{=}126 AI snippets, with the same 18 human solutions used as the baseline for every generator. We evaluate eight LLM judges (Llama 3.1-70B, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Gemini-3-Flash, Ministral-14B, Mistral Large, GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-5-mini, Claude Sonnet 5) at temperature 0.1 0.1 , returning a JSON verdict ( "yes" = LLM-generated, "no" = human-written) with justification; human-written code is the positive class. Each query is repeated three times and averaged. We assess four prompting strategies: ❶ Direct zero-shot classification; ❷ Lexical-guided , extracting comments, identifiers, keywords, and libraries first; ❸ Structural-guided , examining control-flow and formatting first; and ❹ Lexico-semantic-guided , combining lexical cues with inferred purpose and semantics first.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusion
sections.text: We examined whether general-purpose LLMs can serve as training-free judges of code provenance (RQ1) and how feature-guided prompting affects their reliability (RQ2). Zero-shot judging is highly model-dependent: GPT-5-mini achieves strong discrimination, while several judges collapse toward a single class despite near-chance accuracy. Feature-guided prompting is not uniformly beneficial: it recovers collapsed judges such as Llama but degrades the strongest zero-shot judge, GPT-5-mini. Judgments also vary markedly by generator, suggesting sensitivity to generator-specific style rather than a universal AI/human signal. LLM-based provenance judges should therefore be validated per model and generator, not selected from aggregate scores alone. Future work should examine hybrid human-AI code and provenance-preserving transformations.

sections.heading: Data-Availability Statement
sections.text: The data used in this research are derived from publicly available sources. To ensure transparency and reproducibility, the source code, datasets, and usage instructions are publicly accessible on Zenodo ( Djire, 2026 ) .

Adaptability therefore does not remove the need for judge- and prompt-specific validation. Finding 3: Accuracy can mask biased detectors. The dedicated detectors’ 0.50 accuracy looks like chance performance, but F ​ 1 s ​ c ​ o ​ r ​ e = 0.00 F1_{score}{=}0.00 reveals near-constant “AI” predictions. Accuracy alone therefore neither diagnoses class bias nor establishes transfer. Finding 4: Per-language sensitivity is judge-specific. C++ is Claude’s weakest language under every prompting condition, while GPT-5-mini stays largely language-invariant throughout; Llama and Mistral-Large both flip C++ from their worst language under zero-shot/lexical prompting to their best under structural/stylo-semantic guidance, showing that richer context can reshape which language a judge finds easiest rather than uniformly improving all of them. Conclusion We examined whether general-purpose LLMs can serve as training-free judges of code provenance (RQ1) and how feature-guided prompting affects their reliability (RQ2). Zero-shot judging is highly model-dependent: GPT-5-mini achieves strong discrimination, while several judges collapse toward a single class despite near-chance accuracy. Feature-guided prompting is not uniformly beneficial: it recovers collapsed judges such as Llama but degrades the strongest zero-shot judge, GPT-5-mini. Judgments also vary markedly by generator, suggesting sensitivity to generator-specific style rather than a universal AI/human signal. LLM-based provenance judges should therefore be validated per model and generator, not selected from aggregate scores alone. Future work should examine hybrid human-AI code and provenance-preserving transformations. Data-Availability Statement The data used in this research are derived from publicly available sources.
